title: Diversification & Asset Allocation
description: Spread out, then match the mix to the date you need the money.
wolfLine: One company is a bet. A mix is a plan.

diversification.definition: Spreading your money across lots of different investments, so one bad one cannot sink you.
diversification.example: An index fund that holds hundreds of companies.

concentration-risk.definition: Having too much money in one place. If that one thing fails, you lose a lot.
concentration-risk.example: All your savings in the company you work for.

asset-allocation.definition: How you split a portfolio among types of investments, such as stocks and bonds. The split follows the timeline.
asset-allocation.example: 80% stocks and 20% bonds for a goal that is decades away.

rebalancing.definition: Putting the split back to its target after markets move it. You sell some of what grew and buy some of what lagged.
rebalancing.example: Stocks grew to 90% of a portfolio whose target is 80%. Selling the extra 10% is rebalancing.

lessons.title: Diversification
lessons.summary: Don’t let one bad bet sink the pack.

steps.context: [[Diversification]] means spreading your money across lots of different investments, so one bad one can’t sink you.
steps.prompt: Which portfolio is more diversified?
choices: All your money in one company
An index fund holding hundreds of companies
Three companies in the same industry
steps.explain: Hundreds of companies means no single one can wipe you out. That spread is [[diversification]].

steps.context: Having too much money in one place is called [[concentration risk]]. If that one thing fails, you lose big.
steps.prompt: Which of these has the most concentration risk?
choices: A mix of stocks and bonds
All your savings in the company you work for
steps.explain: [[Concentration risk]] is the pile in one place. If that company struggles, the job and the savings can fail together.

steps.prompt: A diversified portfolio can never lose money.
steps.explain: When everything falls, it falls too. Just less painfully than one bad bet.

steps.prompt: Match each way to diversify with an example.
Why mix stocks and bonds in one portfolio?
choices: They often move differently, which smooths out the ride
steps.explain: When one dips, the other often holds steadier. The mix is not a promise.

steps.prompt: Spreading your money across many investments is called ___.
steps.explain: Spread out so no single hit takes you down.

story.title: Two piles
story.body:
Dee has two piles of **$5,000**. One is a house down payment in **3 years**. The other is retirement in about **35 years**.

The 3-year pile stays mostly cash. The 35-year pile can be mostly stocks.

steps.title: Meet Dee
steps.body:
Dee is 29 and a dental hygienist. She has two piles, $5,000 each. One is a house down payment in 3 years. The other is retirement in about 35 years.

[[Asset allocation]] is the split. The 3-year pile wants to stay mostly cash. The 35-year pile can hold mostly [[stock]]s, with some [[bond]]s.

steps.prompt: Which pile can hold mostly stocks?
choices: The house money she needs in 3 years
The retirement money she will not use for about 35 years
Both, because stocks cannot fall for 3 years
steps.explain: Decades can ride out drops. Three years cannot.

steps.prompt: Dee’s house pile is $5,000 and she keeps it in cash. How many dollars of that pile are not in stocks?
steps.explain: All $5,000 stays out of stocks. The timeline is too short.

steps.prompt: The same split fits every goal, no matter when you need the money.
steps.explain: Asset allocation follows the timeline. Soon money and later money are different jobs.

steps.prompt: What is asset allocation?
choices: The split among types of investments
steps.explain: Stocks, bonds, and cash, in proportions that match when you need the money.

steps.title: Two familiar mixes
steps.body: A mix that is 90% [[stock]]s and 10% [[bond]]s will usually swing more in a bad year than a mix that is 60% stocks and 40% bonds. Historically, on average, the stock-heavier mix has also grown more over many decades. That is the trade. It is not a forecast for next year.

steps.prompt: Which mix usually swings more in a single bad year?
choices: They are required to fall the same amount
steps.explain: More stocks, wider swings. The bonds are the calmer slice.

steps.prompt: A $10,000 portfolio is 60% stocks. How many dollars are in stocks?
steps.explain: 0.60 × $10,000 = $6,000. The other $4,000 is the bond slice.

steps.prompt: The same $10,000 is 90% stocks. How many dollars are in stocks?
The calmer mix is always the better one.
steps.explain: Calmer fits a nearer goal. A far-off goal can accept the wider swing for the chance of more growth.

steps.title: The target drifted
steps.body: Your target [[asset allocation]] is 80% stocks and 20% bonds, on $10,000. Stocks had a big year. You now have $9,000 in stocks and $1,000 in bonds. Stocks are 90% of the pile. [[Rebalancing]] sells some of what grew and buys some of what lagged, back to the target.

steps.prompt: On $10,000, how many dollars of stocks is an 80% target?
You have $9,000 in stocks and the target is $8,000. How many dollars of stocks do you sell?
Bonds are $1,000 and the 20% target on $10,000 is $2,000. How many dollars of bonds do you buy?
steps.explain: $2,000 − $1,000 = $1,000. The sale of stocks pays for the bonds.

steps.prompt: Rebalancing means chasing whatever rose the most and buying more of it.
steps.explain: It does the opposite. You trim what grew past the target and top up what fell behind.

lessons.title: Other Countries
lessons.summary: Home is not the whole list.

steps.title: Beyond one country
steps.body: A fund of US companies is [[diversification]] across those companies. It is not diversification across the world. Other countries have other companies, other currencies, and other bad years. Adding them does not promise a higher return. It means one country’s slump is not your entire stock pile.

steps.prompt: A fund that holds only US companies is diversified across what?
choices: Many US companies, and not the rest of the world
Stocks and bonds in equal parts
steps.explain: Many companies, one country. International funds are the other countries.

steps.prompt: Adding international stocks guarantees a smoother year.
steps.explain: Other markets fall too, sometimes in the same year. The point is that they are not the same bet.

steps.prompt: Why include countries besides your own?
choices: So one country’s bad decade is not the whole stock pile
Because a US fund is illegal
steps.explain: The world is a bigger list. It is still stocks, with stock risk.

steps.prompt: A $10,000 stock pile is 70% US and 30% international. How many dollars are international?

lessons.title: Risk Tolerance
lessons.summary: The timeline, and whether you can sleep.

steps.title: Two questions
steps.body: Risk tolerance is how much of a drop you can hold through. The timeline still comes first. A 30-year goal can use a wide swing even if a bad month feels awful. A 2-year goal cannot, no matter how calm you feel today.

steps.prompt: Which timeline is this money on?
items: A house down payment in 2 years
Money you will not touch until your 60s
steps.explain: Soon money stays steady. Decades can take the stock swings.

steps.prompt: You feel brave, and you need the money in 18 months. What wins?
steps.explain: Feeling brave does not make a short timeline long. The bill still arrives.

steps.prompt: A long timeline means a crash will not bother you.
steps.explain: It can bother you. The long timeline means you do not have to sell during it.

steps.prompt: How much of a drop you can hold through is called risk ___.
steps.explain: Tolerance. It sits next to the timeline. It does not replace it.

lessons.title: A Mix for a Goal
lessons.summary: Pick the page that matches the date.

steps.title: Match the date
steps.body: The two-year page is cash, because a drop would hit the goal. The thirty-year page is 80% stocks and 20% bonds. Same person can own both. The goals are different.

docs.title: Goal in two years
docs.subtitle: The money has a near date

steps.prompt: Which page fits a house down payment in two years?
steps.explain: Two years wants the cash page. The stock-heavy page is for the goal that can wait thirty years.

steps.prompt: On the thirty-year page, how many dollars are in bonds?
steps.explain: The bond slice is $2,000, which is 20% of $10,000.

steps.prompt: The thirty-year mix is also the right mix for the house.
steps.explain: The house date is two years. That page stays in savings.

steps.prompt: What changed between the pages?
choices: The ticker of a single stock
steps.explain: Asset allocation follows the date. One person, two dates, two mixes.

lessons.title: Ben’s Lopsided Portfolio
lessons.summary: The job and the stock are the same bet.

steps.title: One employer, twice
steps.body: Ben is 31 and an electrician. $8,000 of his $10,000 portfolio is stock in the company that pays him. If that company stumbles, he can lose the job and the $8,000 together. That is [[concentration risk]].

doc.title: Ben’s portfolio
doc.subtitle: Most of it rides on one employer

lines.label: Stock in the company that employs him

steps.prompt: Which line is the concentration?
steps.explain: The $8,000 employer stock is the pile in one place. The broad fund is the smaller, spread-out line.

steps.prompt: What percent of Ben’s $10,000 is the employer stock?
What is the danger in that 80%?
choices: The broad fund might be boring
A bad year for the employer can hit his paycheck and his portfolio
steps.explain: The job and the stock are the same company. Diversification wants them unlinked.

steps.prompt: Ben is diversified because he also owns $2,000 of a broad fund.
steps.explain: The $2,000 helps a little. $8,000 in one employer is still the concentrated pile.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Diversification & Asset Allocation
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: A $20,000 portfolio targets 70% stocks. How many dollars of stocks is that?
Rebalancing means buying more of whatever just went up.
steps.explain: You trim what grew past the target and add to what fell behind it.

steps.prompt: Which is the clearest concentration risk?
choices: 90% of your portfolio in your employer’s stock
A mix of stocks and bonds
steps.explain: One employer can take the job and the savings in the same bad year.

steps.prompt: Stocks drifted to $9,000 of a $10,000 portfolio. The target is $7,500. How many dollars of stocks do you sell to get back?
